title: Silent japa
hook: Valmiki's mara-mara; the mantra without the mouth
carry: japa goes inward until it says itself

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri, kept at dawn the way Rama kept it. Your line was sandhya: the Gayatri, kept at dawn. Today, the mantra goes quiet.

You know how a song gets stuck in your head? You didn't decide to hum it. You're brushing your teeth and there it is, playing by itself. Annoying, when it's an advertising jingle. But what if it were something you'd chosen? Hindu tradition noticed this long ago, and it tells a story about a robber whose mantra started saying itself.
screen: `A SONG STUCK IN YOUR HEAD.` → `WHAT IF YOU CHOSE THE SONG?` → `A ROBBER'S MANTRA.`

segments.voice: Remember Valmiki, the robber from day seven, who sat so long an anthill grew over him? A much-loved later telling says what he was doing in there. The sage gave him a name to repeat: Rama. But the robber couldn't get it out; the holy name stuck in a mouth used to threats. So the sage said: then say it backwards. Mara. Mara, mara, mara. Say it fast and listen: maramaramara turns into rama, rama, rama. The name was saying itself, and he sat so still the ants built over him. Here's the teaching behind it. Japa, repeating a sacred name, comes three ways. Out loud, as you did with Hare Krishna, is vachika. Whispered, lips moving, barely a sound, is upamshu. Silent, only in the mind, is manasika. Many old texts and teachers rank the silent one highest: the quieter it gets, the deeper it goes in, with no sound to lean on. And past that is ajapa. The a at the front means not: not-repeating. Many yoga teachers say the breath already carries a mantra, a soft so on the in-breath and ham on the out: so-ham, I am that. You can't force ajapa. You start with silent japa, let go, and listen for it. So when a grandmother's lips move without a sound all the way to the store, she isn't mumbling. She's on Valmiki's road: from the lips, inward, until the name says itself.
screen: `VALMIKI: MARA, MARA, MARA…` · `…RAMA, RAMA, RAMA.` · `SPOKEN, WHISPERED, SILENT.` · `AJAPA — NOT-REPEATING.` · then, large: `JAPA GOES INWARD UNTIL IT SAYS ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Settle into your breath and say your mantra silently, the one that fits or simply so-ham: so as you breathe in, ham as you breathe out, no lips, no whisper. After a while, stop saying it on purpose and just listen for the so and the ham in the breath. If you lose it, start saying it again, gently, and let go again.
Ajapa. Not-repeating. The mantra that goes on by itself, carried on the breath: so on the way in, ham on the way out.
Keep this one: japa goes inward until it says itself. Valmiki's name turned around on its own. Day one hundred nine.

howItsDone: Hindu practitioners do japa aloud, whispered or silently in the mind; many meditation lineages teach so-ham (hamsa) with the breath, describing the ajapa japa as the mantra the breath repeats on its own.

Which sound goes with which breath: some teach so on the in-breath and ham on the out (so-ham); others the reverse (ham-sa). Script says 'some teachers say'. Confirm.
